title: Why We Call Them the Valeoran Ruins
subtitle: Valeor, Maera, Endros, and a borrowed name
summary: An old myth from the Scholastic Coast of the god who held Sea and Sky apart, the seafarer he loved and the son who sailed after him, and why Vernan scholars borrowed their names for the ruins and the settlement.
content:
> *"Valeoran is a designation, not an identification."*
> — a Vernan archaeologist's habitual correction

Everyone in Endros says **the Valeoran Ruins**, and almost everyone, sooner or later, asks the obvious question: who, or what, was Valeor? The answer is a story, and a naming decision, and a careful line that Vernan scholars would very much like everyone to keep in mind.

The names of both the **Valeoran Ruins** and the settlement of **Endros** come from an old myth of **Valeor**, **Maera** and their son **Endros**. They were chosen by scholars of the [[university-of-verna|University of Verna]] as **deliberate mythological analogies**. They do **not** mean that the builders of the ruins had anything to do with Valeor, Maera, Endros or the myth. Nothing found so far suggests they did.

## A Myth from the Old Scholastic Coast

The story of Valeor belongs to the **Old Scholastic Coast**, the string of learned cities whose schools were closed in the [[silencing-of-the-schools|Silencing of the Schools]]. Alongside its philosophy, mathematics, astronomy, medicine and natural philosophy, the Coast preserved a great deal of poetry and mythic literature, and the Valeor cycle seems to have been part of that inheritance.

When the Coast's scholars fled to Verna, they carried the story with them: in old coastal manuscripts, later commentaries, fragments and oral tradition. The myth became part of the University's intellectual inheritance, and Verna is now one of the main places where it is studied.

What survives is therefore partly a **reconstruction**. How old the myth is, which city first preserved it, what language its oldest form was in, and whether every surviving version descends from one source are all uncertain. Scholars disagree, sometimes sharply. Some important manuscripts may survive only in Kharadi collections, since the Coast later fell to the older Kharadi regime, and a Kharadi archive may preserve a version that differs from the standard Vernan one. That does not make the myth Kharadi. It reflects how tangled the Coast's history became.

## Valeor and the Raising of the Sky

In the myth, the world was once caught between the **Sea below** and the **Sky above**. They pressed so closely together that there was no true space between them in which mortal life could grow.

**Valeor**, an ancient divine figure, took on the task of separating them. He raised the Sky away from the Sea and held the two apart. In the distance he opened there was room at last for land, weather, travel, settlements and mortal life.

> *Valeor lifted the Sky away from the Sea, so that mortals could live between them.*

Valeor is remembered through images of height, burden, immense strength, separation, the horizon, the sea and the sky. Much else about him is uncertain. The surviving traditions do not agree on his divine family, his place in any larger cosmology, or whether he is imagined as still holding the Sky somewhere, and no complete pantheon has been recovered around him.

## Maera the Seafarer

**Maera** was mortal, and a **seafarer in her own right**. She knew ships, winds, currents and navigation. Valeor loved her, and they had a child.

Maera is not a footnote to the myth. She is its human half: the sea, skill, mortality, and the decision to sail beyond familiar shores. How she and Valeor met is told differently in different versions, and the oldest form of the story does not survive to settle it.

> **A popular retelling, not a preserved verse**
>
> The boy was tangled in the sheet again, and the boat was drifting broadside to the swell.
>
> "You cannot command the sea," Maera told him.
>
> "My father commands the sky."
>
> "Then ask your father to teach you the sky." She took the line out of his hands and showed him, again, how to let it run. "On my ship, you learn the sea."

## Endros

Their son, **Endros**, is remembered as a heroic, semi-divine figure: divine through Valeor, mortal through Maera. He belongs entirely to neither world. He stands between the divine and the mortal, between Sea and Sky, between home and the horizon.

Stories credit him with many mighty deeds, voyages, impossible challenges and feats of endurance. They do not agree on a fixed list, and no single cycle of his adventures has survived intact. It is enough to say that Endros became renowned for many legendary accomplishments before he set out on his last voyage.

A modern line that sums up what he took from each parent is quoted often enough that people sometimes assume it is ancient. It is not, as far as anyone knows:

> *Valeor gave Endros the blood of the divine. Maera taught him how to sail.*

## The Last Voyage

In the end, Endros attempted something greater than all his earlier deeds. He sailed into the unknown **in search of his father**.

Where he was going is not clear. Different versions say he sailed beyond the known seas, toward the horizon, toward the place where Sea and Sky meet, or toward wherever Valeor still carried his burden. Some versions say Valeor called to him; others that he went because he had to know. No version settles what happened to him.

Endros did not come back in any way that answered the question. Nobody knows whether he died, was lost, crossed beyond the known world, reached Valeor, found his father, or simply chose not to return. **The myth ends in uncertainty**, and every serious retelling leaves it there.

## The First Survey

The Ruins were found by a University of Verna vessel taking oceanographic measurements, far from any trade route, any shore and any explored land; that is why nobody had seen them before. When its scholars first documented the enormous ancient structures above the still ocean, they saw something that recalled the old story at once: vast, impossible fragments **suspended between Sea and Sky**, held in place by nothing anyone could explain.

> **A dramatised reconstruction of the first survey**
>
> The researcher at the rail had not said anything for some time. Then, quietly:
>
> "Valeor."
>
> Her colleague looked up from his instruments. "That is dramatic."
>
> "Look at them."
>
> He looked. He did not argue.

## Why "Valeoran"

The term **Valeoran** began as a scholarly analogy, and it means *resembling, or evocative of, Valeor*. It does **not** mean *built by Valeor*, and it does **not** mean *belonging to a people called the Valeorans*. There is no evidence that the builders knew the myth, called themselves anything like Valeoran, or had any connection with Valeor, or that Valeor was ever more than a figure of story.

The name stuck because it was memorable and fitting, and in time it became the standard international designation. Vernan archaeologists have spent years since then explaining what it does not mean.

> **At a public lecture in Endros, during questions**
>
> "So Valeor built them?"
>
> "No."
>
> "Then why call them Valeoran?"
>
> "Because they reminded the first surveyors of Valeor."
>
> "That seems imprecise."
>
> The lecturer sighed. "There was a poet on the survey team."
>
> "Ah."

## Why the Settlement Is Called Endros

As a permanent research settlement grew up around and beneath the ruins, the University kept to the same tradition. If the impossible structure overhead was Valeoran, the mortal settlement below it should be named for Valeor's mortal son: the one who grew up with the sea, lived between worlds and sailed into the unknown.

> **How the naming is usually told (a reconstruction, not a record)**
>
> "If the ruins are Valeoran, the station should have a matching name."
>
> "Valeor Station?"
>
> "No. We are not the ones holding up the sky."
>
> Someone at the end of the table said: "Then Endros."
>
> There was a silence.
>
> "Endros."

Exactly how the name was made official, and who first proposed it, are not recorded in the Archive's sources. What is clear is that the Gates made it far more fitting than anyone intended. Expeditioners do what Endros did on his last voyage: they leave familiar shores, cross into the unknown, pursue things they do not fully understand and travel where maps fail, knowing they may not learn what waits on the other side.

## The Myth Today

The discovery of the ruins revived interest in a story that had been known mainly to scholars. Valeor, Maera and Endros now turn up in newspapers, public lectures, recruitment material, expedition slang, popular songs, political speeches, memorials and religious commentary, and different people reach for different figures:

- **Valeor** stands for burden and for making ordinary life possible: holding danger apart, keeping open the space where people can live. He is a natural figure for engineers, for infrastructure, and for anyone responsible for the Outpost.
- **Maera** stands for mortal courage, seafaring, practical skill and navigation, and is especially loved by sailors, navigators, pilots and expedition crews. She keeps the myth from being only a story about a god and his heroic son.
- **Endros** stands for exploration, ambition, the unknown horizon, the search for answers and the willingness to leave safety behind. His last voyage is read as heroic, tragic, foolish or necessary, depending on who is telling it.

That last ambiguity makes the name both inspiring and ominous, and Expeditioners know it.

> **Two Expeditioners at a Gate threshold**
>
> "You know how Endros's story ends."
>
> "No."
>
> "He disappears."
>
> "Exactly. We don't know how it ends."

## Other Readings of the Ruins

The Valeoran name does not replace anyone else's way of understanding the ruins:

- Some Vardic enthusiasts connect them to the **Nameless King** (see [[old-gods-of-the-holds|The Old Gods of the Holds]]), a theory scholars treat as folklore-driven speculation.
- Tianzhao scholars approach them through their theories of the Spirit and Celestial realms (see [[ten-thousand-offices-of-heaven|The Ten Thousand Offices of Heaven]]).
- Aurelian and Vesperian theologians read them through order and stewardship, or through possibility and revelation (see [[faith-of-the-first-light|The Faith of the First Light]]).
- Many Kharadi scholars use the established name while remaining politely sceptical of the analogy behind it.

## What Archaeologists Actually Know

It is worth being plain about the boundary between story and evidence. **None of the following is established:**

- that Valeor built the ruins;
- that Maera or Endros were historical people;
- that Endros reached the ruins, or crossed a Gate;
- that the myth records an ancient Gate event;
- that the Old Scholastic Coast knew the ruins existed;
- that the ruins inspired the myth.

Theories along those lines exist, and some are popular in Endros's taverns. They are speculation, folklore, fringe archaeology or religious interpretation. The ruins remain what they were when the first surveyors saw them: something impossible, suspended between Sea and Sky, with a borrowed name.
